newsitem.title: USA: Conservatives slam lack of Republican leadership.
newsitem.headline: Conservatives slam lack of Republican leadership.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
About 1,000 conservative activists gathered on Thursday, worried and highly critical about what they called a lack of leadership and direction from the Republican Party.

"Conservatives come here both pleased at the progress we have made but very concerned at the lack of coherent leadership from with the movement and from Congress," said David Keene, chairman of the American Conservative Union.
The activists, meeting under the umbrella of the Conservative Political Action Conference, were to hear from an array of Republican leaders over the next three days.
Keene said some Republicans seemed tempted to stay on the sidelines and keep their mouths shut while Clinton was embroiled in a deepening scandal over campaign fund raising but that was a mistake.
"Republicans in Washington are still upset that they didn't win the White House. They are in a funk,"Ralph Reed, director of the Christian Coalition, also attacked Republican passivity.
"This strategy of timidity, of retreat, of muddle-headed moderation, is a self-defeating strategy," he said. "It leads only to paralysis."

House Speaker Newt Gingrich kicked off the convention, admitting that Republicans seemed to have lost their nerve after last year's elections, in which Democrat President Clinton was re-elected but Republicans kept control of both houses of Congress.

"For the first time in 68 years, we re-elected a Republican House," Gingrich said. But despite that accomplishment, he said, "the winning team feels defeated. People walk around with long jaws and commentators talk about how concerned they are that Republicans have lost their way."
But Gingrich said that was about to change as Republicans put forward a list of legislative goals for the current session of Congress.

However, Gingrich himself, formerly the darling of the conservative movement, is the target of many right-wing complaints. The speaker has adopted an uncharacteristically low profile since he was reprimanded by the House and fined $300,000 for ethical violations.

Conservative columnists Rowland Evans and Robert Novak, in an article distributed to delegates, said: "Increasingly disaffected conservatives say Gingrich's words no longer match his deeds. Disaffection on the right may be the speaker's biggest problem."
Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott is well liked by conservatives, but many feel he lacks the authority and ability to be an effective national spokesman for the party.

Meanwhile, former Republican chairman Haley Barbour, a talented communicator, has stepped down. His replacement Jim Nicholson has been avoided public appearances and has been almost invisible as a spokesman.
Former presidential candidate Lamar Alexander told Reuters that Republicans had no obvious leader and no sense of mission.
"Right now, we're very timid. The president is tip-toeing across the bridge to the future and we're sitting around the campfire," he said.
Millionaire publisher Steve Forbes, another unsuccessful Republican presidential candidate last year, expressed similar sentiments in an interview with Reuters this week.
"What I think is the real vacuum is the lack of an agenda, not just nuts and bolts, but what is the overriding vision?"
Evans and Novak said: "Morale in the GOP (Republican Party) is extremely low ... The Republicans have no clear vision, no agenda and no recognised national leadership."
